items.readable_text:
Content:
Two lines that never cross are said to be parallel. For two lines to be parallel, they must have the same slope.

Content:
For example, the lines [MATH: y=2x+4] and [MATH: y=2x-5] have the same slope of [MATH: m=2,] so they are parallel. Indeed, looking at the graph, we see that the two lines never cross.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c624ae330b1e5f51867eebeb4b2c88d8]

Content:
On the other hand, the lines [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+4] and [MATH: y=2x-5] have different slopes, so they are not parallel. Indeed, looking at the graph, we see that the two lines do cross.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d266c54c63add0e0a2a374d625b5dcae]

sections.normalized_html:
For two lines to be parallel, they must have the same slope.

Both lines are in slope-intercept form, so we can pick out the slope of each equation by looking at the [MATH: x]-coefficient.

  • The slope of the line [MATH: y=cx+7] is [MATH: c.]

  • The slope of the line [MATH: y=5x-3] is [MATH: 5.]

Because the slopes must be the same, we must have [MATH: c=5.]

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following lines is parallel to [MATH: 12x - y=3?]

  1. [MATH: y=4x-8]

  2. [MATH: y=12x+1]

  3. [MATH: y=3x-12]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following lines is parallel to [MATH: 12x - y=3?]

1. [MATH: y=4x-8]
2. [MATH: y=12x+1]
3. [MATH: y=3x-12]

sections.normalized_html:
For two lines to be parallel, they must have the same slope.

To find the slope of the line [MATH: 12x-y=3,] we convert to slope-intercept form:

[MATH: 12x − y|= 3; − y|= − 12x + 3; y|= 12x − 3.]

In slope-intercept form, the slope is the [MATH: x]-coefficient. So, the slope is [MATH: 12.]

From the given options, the only line that has a slope of [MATH: 12] is [MATH: y = 12x+1.]
